content: Hi all, I'm Nathan. I've been learning Lean 4 for a while now, and I'm comfortable writing proofs. Now, I'm looking for a way in to contributing to Mathlib. I have experience using Git and GitHub for my own small projects, but I've never contributed to something of this scale. I'd like to get some experience working in a large shared codebase and going through the full PR process. I can put in roughly 2-3 hours per week for the next month. Can anyone direct me to an entry point or give me tips on how to find one? I'm open to suggestions, but I'd probably be most at home with something in the realm of graph theory, analysis, or optimization.

Welcome! There are lots of stuff to do; could you elaborate on your interests?

Nathan Albin said:

give me tips on how to find one?

Pick a medium-sized goal (e.g. a cool theorem from an introductory book about a subject), think carefully on what it'll take to formalize it, realize that Mathlib is missing easier theorems that you need for your goal, then work on those easier theorems. Rinse and repeat until your actual goal is merged, then find another goal.

I have many tasks in graph theory I could suggest, but I find that the important thing is to keep yourself interested, so I'm not sure about suggesting random lemmas.
Here's something you could try: "Any two longest paths in a preconnected graph intersect". The issue with this one is that the proof seems to be annoying casework or wlog and constructing ugly paths, but I wonder if there's a more general property with a clever proof that'll make this one nice.

Snir Broshi said:

"Any two longest paths in a preconnected graph intersect"

nice puzzle! pedantic correction / clarification "any two longest paths in a finite preconnected graph intersect" (this is probably implicit in "longest")
Do you have a counterexample for infinite graphs?
what does "longest" mean in a graph with infinite paths?
Great! Thanks for the advice!

Aaron Liu said:

what does "longest" mean in a graph with infinite paths?

Hmm, would just infinite work there though ? Would then be “any two infinite paths intersect in a …. pre connected …”
in the lattice Z^2 where (x,y) is connected to (x+1,y) and (x,y+1) it's very easy to make two disjoint infinite paths

Perhaps that’s the counter example asked for then , hard to say , but under a reasonable interpretation I think that could make sense as the ask here.

Besides easy in math can be notoriously hard in Lean , you reckon it would be easy to show that in Lean ?
if you require the paths be finite and that there be no longer finite path then you can reduce to the finite case

Maybe when phrased as “two longest paths induce a connected subgraph “ , interpretation of longest as somehow infinite like that is easier to see as not overly helpful.

As you said in the example essentially remove a point of a (bidirectionally) infinite path to get two non intersecting infinite ones.

Then again such rays are infinite , but in a ray sense , not like Z so no longer bidirectionally infinite . But this is not really about cardinality anymore and something else.

Aaron Liu said:

in the lattice Z^2 where (x,y) is connected to (x+1,y) and (x,y+1) it's very easy to make two disjoint infinite paths

my bad i should have included the counterexample, this is exactly the one i had in mind. this is offtopic now but we don't even really have "infinite paths" — like Aaron says the result is still true for graphs of finite diameter, i think that's the right hypothesis and framing it as "finite graphs" was probably misleading of me

I think it isnt too big of a deal for this thread, as in as a new beginner thread, open ended for suggestions, going into such details is actually probably more helpful for OP not less.

I think as I said above you don't even need to look that specific for a counter example, unless my worded one was wrong.

And yea, theory like that on infinite graphs is sorely missing, at least to have such a precise interface to said paths and the finite/infinite settings to go between.

Ironically , it would be great if OP could get to a stage I could define things like loop-erased random walks, once-reinforced random walks, and other random non-markov processes that highly depend on paths, where questions of interest are about recurrence/transience/F_infinity measurable so its been highly annoying to try get this in Lean, for myself anyway.

FWIW, I know enough about LERWs to have implemented Wilson's algorithm for one of my research projects. That probably doesn't prepare me much for the Lean proof side, but it's at least a concept I'm familiar with and might give some ideas of early directions I could take.

Aaron Liu said:

what does "longest" mean in a graph with infinite paths?

Aaron Liu said:

in the lattice Z^2 where (x,y) is connected to (x+1,y) and (x,y+1) it's very easy to make two disjoint infinite paths

Paths are not infinite, see docs#SimpleGraph.Walk and docs#SimpleGraph.Path.
It might be nice to add it as a separate concept (and also rays), but that wasn't the question I posed.

Thomas Waring said:

like Aaron says the result is still true for graphs of finite diameter, i think that's the right hypothesis

I don't think this hypothesis is necessary, unless you have a counterexample.
Are you saying the hypothesis is necessary because the theorem is vacuous otherwise? as in there is no longest path in a graph of infinite diameter

If you mean not necessary (not sure if the question was for me) then yes, except that the preconnected part is important here so I disagree with the second half (e.g. ⊥ : Fin 2 has infinite diameter yet does have a longest path)
(btw Nathan Albin I didn't mean to make this thread about this specific problem; I could suggest many other things in graph theory, and some in analysis if you're interested)

To slightly bring the thread back: since you've mentioned analysis you could show the integral representation of the Zeta function

import Mathlib
example {s : ℂ} (h : 1 < s.re) :
    riemannZeta s = (1 / Complex.Gamma s) *
      ∫ x in Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ), (x : ℂ) ^ (s - 1) / (Real.exp x - 1) := by
  sorry

or do some calculus:

theorem strictMono_sub_arctan_self : StrictMono fun x ↦ x - Real.arctan x := by
  sorry

example {x n : ℝ} (hn : 0 ≤ n) (h : -n ≤ x) : (1 + x / n) ^ n ≤ x.exp := sorry
example {x n : ℝ} (hx : x ≠ 0) (hn : 0 ≤ n) (h : -n ≤ x) : (1 + x / n) ^ n < x.exp := sorry
example (x : ℝ) : MonotoneOn (fun n : ℝ ↦ (1 + x / n) ^ n) (.Ici <| 0 ⊔ -x) := sorry
example {x : ℝ} (hx : x ≠ 0) : StrictMonoOn (fun n : ℝ ↦ (1 + x / n) ^ n) (.Ici <| 0 ⊔ -x) := sorry

Snir Broshi said:

If you mean not necessary (not sure if the question was for me) then yes, except that the preconnected part is important here so I disagree with the second half (e.g. ⊥ : Fin 2 has infinite diameter yet does have a longest path)

ok i see your point, thanks! my instinct would be to state that the path has length equal to the diameter (in particular finite), but preconnected + all paths shorter than blah is equivalent

Thomas Waring said:

my instinct would be to state that the path has length equal to the diameter

The diameter is not the length of a longest path, e.g. in a complete graph on n > 1 vertices the diameter is 1 but a longest path has length n
oh of course, clearly i have gotten myself quite mixed up & should be ignored on this topic :)
